title: Petit Verdot
description: A late-ripening Bordeaux grape that adds colour and spice to blends, and shines alone in warm places.
L: Describe Petit Verdot's colour and flavours

Petit Verdot is a black grape from Bordeaux. Its small, thick-skinned berries give very deep colour, high tannin and high acidity. It smells of violet, blackberry, blueberry, and spices like clove and sage. In a blend, a few percent is enough to add colour, structure and a floral, spicy lift.

Its name means little green one, because in Bordeaux it often failed to ripen fully. It buds early and ripens very late, often after Cabernet Sauvignon. In cool years, it stayed green and harsh. That's why Bordeaux planted little of it, and used it only as a seasoning in the blend.
It means little green one, because in Bordeaux it often stayed unripe.

In a Bordeaux blend, you may not notice Petit Verdot directly, but it deepens the colour and adds a violet and spice note, and firmer tannin on the finish. Alone, it is inky purple, intense, with violets and dark fruit, firm tannin and fresh acidity.
What does Petit Verdot add to a blend?
Petit Verdot adds acidity, not lowers it.
Petit Verdot gives deep colour, tannin, acidity and spice
Its name means little green one, from struggling to ripen
It seasons Bordeaux blends and can stand alone
Explain why warm climates suit it
Explain its role in Bordeaux today

Petit Verdot is mainly a Left Bank grape, used in small amounts in the Médoc. Château Margaux and others use a few percent. Plantings fell in the 20th century, but warmer vintages since the 1990s have helped it ripen more reliably, and some estates have added more.
A small part of Left Bank blends

In warm, dry places, Petit Verdot ripens fully. Spain grows it in La Mancha and Castilla, sometimes as a single variety. Australia's Riverland and McLaren Vale, California, Virginia and Washington all make varietal Petit Verdot. Argentina and Chile use it in blends.
Why does Petit Verdot do better in warm climates?
It needs a lot of rain
As a late ripener, it needs a long, warm season to reach full ripeness.

With warmer vintages, Petit Verdot is gaining interest in Bordeaux as a grape that keeps acidity in heat. Growers value its freshness and colour as other grapes ripen faster. It's one reason some see it as part of Bordeaux's future blend.
Petit Verdot is mainly a Right Bank grape in Bordeaux.
Not true. It's mostly found in small amounts on the Left Bank, in the Médoc.
Petit Verdot is a minor Left Bank blending grape
Warm regions in Spain, Australia and the US ripen it fully
Climate change has renewed interest in Bordeaux

Made alone, Petit Verdot gives intense, dark wines with violet, blueberry, liquorice and spice, firm tannin and bright acidity. It can be austere young. Warm regions give rounder, riper styles. In Virginia, it has become a signature grape, ripening well in humid summers thanks to loose bunches that resist rot.

Winemakers often pick it late for full ripeness, use gentle extraction to avoid harshness, and age it in oak to soften tannins. Some blend in a little Cabernet or Shiraz to round it out. Its high acidity helps it age, and good examples develop for a decade or more.
Match each region to its Petit Verdot role.
Petit Verdot plays different roles in different places.
If you find a varietal Petit Verdot, decant it. Its tannins open up with air, and the violet aromas become clearer.
Why does Petit Verdot handle Virginia's humid summers?
Thick skins and loose bunches resist rot
Loose bunches let air circulate, reducing rot in humid conditions.
Varietal Petit Verdot is intense, floral and firm
Ripe picking, gentle extraction and oak soften it
Virginia, Australia and Spain make notable examples

Petit Verdot's firm tannin and acidity suit rich, savoury food: lamb with herbs, venison, braised beef, hard aged cheeses. Its floral, spicy notes go well with rosemary, sage and black pepper. Avoid delicate fish and very spicy dishes, which clash with its tannin.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, ideally decanted. Young varietal Petit Verdot can be austere; three to five years in bottle softens it. Good examples age 10 to 15 years. In blends, it helps Bordeaux age longer by adding acidity and tannin.
Decant; three to five years to soften
Petit Verdot's floral notes pair well with herbs like rosemary and ____.
Sage and rosemary echo its savoury, floral side.

Good Petit Verdot balances its tannin and acidity with ripe fruit; underripe examples taste green and harsh. Look for producers in warm regions or top Bordeaux estates. As a varietal, it's still niche, so it often offers value for its intensity.
Young varietal Petit Verdot can taste austere and benefits from time.
Yes. Its tannin and acidity soften with a few years in bottle or with decanting.
Petit Verdot suits lamb, game and herb-crusted meat
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees and decant
It softens with age; the best last 10 to 15 years
Explain its role alone and in blends
What does Petit Verdot add to Bordeaux blends?
Small amounts add colour, structure and a floral, spicy lift.
Petit Verdot ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon.
Not true. It ripens very late, often after Cabernet.
Match each fact to Petit Verdot.
Its story connects Bordeaux to new homes.
Which regions make varietal Petit Verdot?
Champagne grows Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.
Petit Verdot needs a long, ____ season to ripen.
As a late ripener, warmth is essential.
Petit Verdot is dark, tannic, acidic and floral
